units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So, can I ask a rude question about the biggest museum in the country?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Always.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Why does it look like a cathedral that took a wrong turn?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ha. People said that when it opened.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Really?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Really. The architect was Pierre Cuypers, a Catholic from the south of the Netherlands.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The museum opened in 1885. Some Protestant critics in Amsterdam thought it looked far too much like a church.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: To a country that had spent centuries being proudly Protestant.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not quite proudly. Very, very seriously.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Fair.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And here's a thing. Cuypers also designed Amsterdam Central Station.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait. Both buildings?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Both. The station where you arrived, and the museum where you're standing.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Same architect, same red brick, same fussy towers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So he basically bookended the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More or less. The station is the front door, and this is the family treasure room.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, where are we exactly?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You should be on the side facing Museumplein, the big lawn behind the museum, or at the main entrance.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With a ticket for one o'clock, you go to the entrance, and you go in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We'll tell you the story while you queue, or later, if you pause us.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the collection started where?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not in Amsterdam. In 1800 it was founded in The Hague, as a national gallery.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then it moved.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1808. Louis Bonaparte, Napoleon's brother, was king of the Netherlands, and he moved it to Amsterdam.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For a while, it lived in the Royal Palace on the Dam.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then in a different old building, and finally here.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A museum that had to find a home.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Like a very expensive student.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ha. Okay, so what do I look at?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Let's choose three things, because nobody can see all of it in an afternoon.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Three. Bet I get one right.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Go on.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The Night Watch.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. Rembrandt, finished in 1642.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And here's something people get wrong.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: It's not at night.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's not at night.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ben!

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a daytime scene. Over the centuries, the varnish darkened and the painting looked like a night scene, and the name stuck.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The real title is much longer, something like the militia company of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So a group portrait of a neighborhood militia.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exactly. Amsterdam's civic guard companies commissioned group portraits, and Rembrandt made his dramatic instead of lined up in rows.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And people liked that?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: History is mixed. We do know it's a huge painting, and it was cut down on the sides, in 1715, when it moved to the Town Hall on the Dam, because it didn't fit between two doors.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait. They cut a Rembrandt to fit a wall?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They did.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That is the least Dutch thing I've ever heard, and the most Dutch.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Practical to the bone. Look at the faces, and look for the girl in yellow, who gets lots of attention.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Our advice is to go there first, before the crowds thicken.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the other two?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Something quieter. Vermeer's painting of a kitchen maid pouring milk.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's small, and everybody who sees it stops talking.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the third is for the spooky request.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Right. You wanted spooky.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I did.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: So find a vanitas. That's a type of still life, very popular in the Netherlands in the seventeenth century.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A table with fruit, flowers, a pocket watch, sometimes a skull.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A skull on a table.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As a reminder. The word means emptiness, or vanity.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The message is that wealth and beauty don't last, so enjoy them but don't be fooled.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Latin phrase is memento mori, remember you will die.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's very cheerful for a lunch break.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To be fair, it was the opposite of a threat.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was a gentle reminder, painted by artists who were selling to rich merchants.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Rich merchants who wanted a skull above the fireplace.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Next to the silver. Yes.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, I love it. What else?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The model rooms. A cabinet house of the early eighteenth century, with tiny furniture, belonging to a woman named Petronella Oortman.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It cost about as much as a real house.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A toy house the price of a house.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the Gallery of Honour, the long hall leading to the Night Watch.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's the museum's spine.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I've heard about the bicycles.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ah. The passage.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: There is a passage?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's a tunnel under the central part of the building, with a public road and a bike path.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For over a hundred years, people have cycled and walked straight through the museum.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Through it, not around it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And when the museum was rebuilt, with work that started in 2003 and finished in 2013, a long ten years, a plan to close the passage ran into the cycling lobby.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Of course.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Of course. They won, and the passage stayed open.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the national treasure house has a bike lane.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it works. When you walk out the door, you'll see.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. How long do we stay?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Your ticket is for one o'clock.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Two hours is comfortable. Three if you love it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's a garden outside, free to walk into, with sculptures, if you need air.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And then we leave through the back and go onto the lawn.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Pause here as long as you like, and when you're out, press play.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Ben, one thing. A small question for the audience.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Go ahead.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Look at the Night Watch, and count the hands in the painting.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Oh, that's good.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I'm going to lose count.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll lose count, and you'll lose track of time.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Go.
